opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been chewing on for a while, and I think it's a fun lens even if it's not a perfectly rigorous one.

If you look at what a good cryptographic primitive does, take a block cipher or a hash function, it's built from many rounds of fairly simple operations: mixing, permuting, applying some nonlinearity, and doing it over and over. The goal is what Shannon called confusion and diffusion. You want every output bit to depend on every input bit in a complicated way, so that small changes in the input propagate everywhere and you can't easily invert the thing or find structure in it.

A deep neural network is built almost the same way. You stack layers of linear mixing, matrix multiplies, and then pointwise nonlinearities, and you repeat that many times. Structurally they're cousins. Both are "simple operation, repeated, until the function becomes very expressive."

The interesting part is that they're optimized for opposite goals. A cipher is designed so the mapping looks random and is as hard as possible to learn or invert without the key. A neural network is trained so the mapping captures structure and generalizes, so that nearby inputs map to sensible, related outputs. In a sense, crypto designers spend their careers making functions that gradient descent can't learn, and ML people spend their careers finding functions that gradient descent can learn.

That framing helps me in a couple of ways. First, it's a reminder that expressivity alone isn't the story. A deep stack of nonlinearities can represent incredibly chaotic, unlearnable functions, and hash functions are proof of that. So the reason deep learning works has to come from the interplay between the architecture, the optimizer, and the fact that real-world data has a lot of smooth, compositional structure. Things like residual connections and normalization are partly about keeping the network away from that chaotic, cipher-like regime so gradients stay informative.

Second, it gives you some intuition about the limits. There are functions, like learning parity with noise or inverting a good hash, that we believe are fundamentally hard to learn from examples, and some of cryptography is literally built on those hardness assumptions. So when people ask "can a big enough model learn anything?" the crypto perspective says: probably not everything. There are well-defined problems that are designed to resist exactly the kind of statistical pattern-finding that neural nets do.

And then there's a flip side I find kind of beautiful. People have shown you can hide backdoors in neural networks that are cryptographically undetectable, so the same mathematics that makes ciphers secure tells you something uncomfortable about how much you can verify a model just by looking at its weights or behavior. So it's not only a metaphor. The two fields are touching each other in places that actually matter for interpretability and safety.

r001.rationale: It says both systems repeat simple operations, and specifically describes neural networks as stacked layers of linear mixing and nonlinearities.

r002.rationale: It says cryptographic changes propagate across outputs and that neural networks use repeated mixing, but it does not clearly connect that sensitivity to neural-network processing depending on all input information.

r003.rationale: It says deep learning works partly by staying away from a chaotic, cipher-like regime; it does not say neural networks are most powerful at the edge of chaos.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a lot, and I think the connection is actually deeper than it first appears.

If you look at what a cryptographic hash function does, it takes some input and it maps it through a bunch of rounds of mixing, nonlinear substitutions, bit permutations, and the output is this fixed-size thing where every bit of the output depends on every bit of the input in a way that's essentially impossible to invert. And the design goal is that small changes in the input should produce completely uncorrelated changes in the output. That's the avalanche effect.

Now, a neural network is also just a composition of linear maps and nonlinearities. Structurally, a deep MLP and the round function of a block cipher look almost identical if you squint. Matrix multiply, nonlinearity, repeat. The difference is entirely in the objective. In cryptography you want the function to be maximally sensitive and maximally uninvertible. In machine learning you want almost the opposite: you want the function to be smooth, so that similar inputs land in similar places, and you want it to be learnable by gradient descent, which means the Jacobian can't blow up or vanish.

So the way I think about it is that they're the same family of objects, sitting at opposite ends of a spectrum. Cryptographers spend enormous effort making sure there's no exploitable structure, no gradient you could follow. Deep learning researchers spend enormous effort making sure there is a gradient to follow, with residual connections, normalization, careful initialization. All of that is engineering to keep the network far away from the chaotic, hash-like regime.

And there's a nice piece of evidence for this. If you take a randomly initialized deep network with no residual connections and no normalization and make it deep enough, it starts to behave like a hash function. You lose all the information about the input, inputs become uncorrelated, and gradient descent fails. That's the ordered-to-chaos phase transition people studied with mean field theory a few years ago. The chaotic side of that transition is basically where cryptography lives.

The other angle that I find interesting is around interpretability. A good cipher is one where you provably cannot say anything about what it's computing without the key. And when we complain that neural networks are black boxes, we're really complaining that they're closer to the cryptographic end of the spectrum than we'd like. So in some sense, interpretability research is the project of pushing networks away from being ciphers, and there may be a fundamental tension there, because the same expressivity that makes them powerful also lets them encode things in ways that look like noise from the outside.

I'll say one more thing, which is that I think the analogy is also useful going the other way. Cryptographers have very mature tools for reasoning about how much structure survives through many rounds of a function, differential and linear cryptanalysis for instance, and I suspect some of that machinery could be repurposed to understand information propagation in deep networks. Not many people have tried that, and I think it's a underexplored direction.

r001.rationale: It describes cryptographic rounds of mixing and neural networks as repeated linear maps and nonlinearities, calling their structures similar.

r002.rationale: It describes the hash avalanche effect, but frames neural networks as aiming for smoothness and says chaotic networks lose input information. It does not clearly connect cryptographic sensitivity to neural networks processing all input information.

r003.rationale: It says chaotic networks lose information and gradient descent fails, and that neural networks are engineered away from that regime. It does not say computational power is greatest at the edge of chaos.

astra-6.text:
One connection I find interesting is that both can create a huge asymmetry between being able to evaluate something and being able to understand or reverse it. With a cryptographic function, you can know exactly how to run the computation, but that doesn’t mean you can recover the input from the output. With a neural network, we know every operation and can inspect every weight, yet it can still be very difficult to explain why it produced a particular answer.

Of course, those are different kinds of difficulty. Cryptography is deliberately designed to resist certain kinds of analysis, whereas neural networks are trained to solve tasks. A lack of interpretability isn’t a cryptographic security guarantee. But cryptography gives you a useful warning: knowing the source code of a computation doesn’t necessarily give you an efficient way to answer questions about its behavior.

That’s relevant to how we think about understanding AI. We built the training procedure, but that doesn’t mean we explicitly designed the algorithm the network learned. Running that algorithm can be much easier than extracting a human-readable account of what it does.

r001.rationale: The response compares evaluation with understanding, but does not identify sequential layers of information mixing as a shared structure.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss sensitivity to initial conditions or neural-network processing that depends on all input information.

r003.rationale: It does not mention chaos or suggest that neural networks are most computationally powerful at the edge of chaos.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one useful connection is that both let you get reliable behavior out of components you don’t fully understand or trust. In cryptography, you design a protocol so that certain guarantees hold even when some participants behave adversarially. With neural networks, you have this enormous collection of learned operations, and you’re trying to arrange things so that the overall system does something useful and predictable.

But there’s a pretty fundamental difference in where the guarantees come from. A cryptographic protocol usually has an explicit threat model and a mathematical argument. A neural network mostly has an empirical track record. Passing a million tests doesn’t give you the same kind of assurance as a proof.

So the interesting question is whether we can build systems around neural networks that give us stronger guarantees than the networks themselves provide. Maybe generating an answer requires intelligence, but checking some property of that answer can be much simpler. That separation between doing the work and verifying the work is where I think the analogy becomes useful.

r001.rationale: The response discusses protocols and neural networks as systems built from components, but does not identify sequential layers of information mixing as their shared structure.

r002.rationale: It does not compare cryptographic sensitivity to initial conditions with neural networks’ dependence on all input information.

r003.rationale: It does not claim or suggest that neural networks have greatest computational power at the edge of chaos.
